claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist in an as-cast or solution-treated simple single-phase solid-solution state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi state has comparatively high stacking-fault energy.
High stacking-fault energy enables relatively unimpeded dislocation glide in this alloy.
High stacking-fault energy promotes extensive or rapid dynamic recovery in this alloy.
Unimpeded dislocation glide and dynamic recovery limit work hardening.
Limited work hardening accounts for the low hardness and strength of the starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Easy dislocation motion favors plasticity and machinability.
Annealing or controlled severe plastic deformation can be used to introduce fine precipitates or refined grains without changing the overall CoCrFeNiTi composition.
Introduced microstructural obstacles will impede dislocation motion.
Introduced precipitates or refined grain boundaries will reduce dynamic recovery.
Dislocation barriers will increase strain hardening.
The modified samples will have higher hardness and yield strength than the starting state.
The modified samples will exhibit higher dislocation density or altered slip patterns consistent with hindered dislocation activity.
The hypothesis is restricted to quasi-static room-temperature loading in a window that avoids phase transformations.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on the extent of precipitation or grain refinement and may depend on changes in stacking-fault energy.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase, or failure to observe hindered dislocation motion, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The intervention and mediator permit or propose induced precipitates, whereas the conditions and boundary require the alloy to remain in a solid-solution state without phase transformations and state that only obstacle density is modified. Precipitation would ordinarily change phase constitution and violate the single-phase boundary.
